title: Automated classical van't Hoff analysis of large-scale chromatographic retention data
content: Classical van't Hoff analysis remains one of the most widely used approaches for describing the temperature dependence of chromatographic retention, yet its application is commonly based on manually assembled retention series and individually evaluated regressions. Here, we present a modular R workflow for automated van't Hoff analysis of large chromatographic retention datasets. The workflow operates downstream of automated chromatogram processing and converts retention tables into quality-controlled temperature series grouped by compound and chromatographic conditions. Replicate measurements and multiple detector wavelengths are consolidated before fitting linear relationships between ln k and 1/T. An optional externally supplied hold-up time, which may be global, column-specific, or temperature-dependent, enables consistent recalculation of retention factors, and its uncertainty is propagated into the fitted enthalpies; phase-ratio information can be incorporated when available. Isolated anomalous observations are detected using externally studentized residuals gated by a dataset-level (baseline) residual scale and remain explicitly retained in diagnostic outputs and plots. The workflow provides apparent van't Hoff enthalpies with confidence intervals, fit-quality and lack-of-fit metrics, optional entropy and Gibbs free-energy estimates when the phase ratio is known, and derived descriptors expressing absolute and relative changes in retention factor and selectivity per unit temperature. Custom heatmaps enable rapid comparison across compounds, stationary phases, eluents, and temperatures. Application to a multi-column HPLC dataset containing eight pharmaceutical analytes measured between 10 to 40 °C demonstrates the scalability of the approach, and Monte Carlo simulations based on the residual scale of this dataset quantify the false-exclusion and detection rates of the automated decisions. The method does not alter the assumptions of classical van't Hoff analysis, but provides a transparent, reproducible, and extensible framework for its automated application to large chromatographic datasets.
